title: What We Get Wrong About Being Understood
author: Greg McKeown
summary: Greg McKeown argues that what most people mean by 'being understood' is actually being agreed with — and that this confusion makes genuine understanding nearly impossible. He cites a 2024 Psychological Science study across 11 studies with 3,396 adults showing that people routinely rate disagreeing listeners as worse listeners, even when those listeners display all the behavioral markers of attentive listening. The practical implication: 'You're not listening' often means 'You're not agreeing.' McKeown illustrates the cost of conflating understanding with agreement through the story of Anwar Sadat, who flew to Jerusalem in 1977 not because he agreed with Israel but because he refused to let disagreement make understanding impossible — and who prepared for that act by spending 18 months in prison confronting his own inner anger, pride, and grievance. The article offers a concrete practice: before agreeing or disagreeing with anyone, use the seven most important words — 'Let me see if I understand you.'
points: The single most clarifying reframe in the article: the opposite of disagreement is not agreement, it is understanding. Most conversations collapse because people rush through the space between the two, treating failure to agree as a failure to listen.

A 2024 Psychological Science study found that across 11 studies and 3,396 adults, speakers consistently rated disagreeing listeners as worse listeners even when those listeners demonstrated genuine attentiveness. 'You're not listening' often means 'You're not agreeing.'

Understanding requires willingness to stay in the space between agree and disagree long enough to see what you could not see before — a discipline that Sadat practiced by confronting his own anger, grievance, and pride before he could cross into enemy territory.

Sadat's visit to Jerusalem in 1977 was not an act of surrender or agreement: it was an act of understanding that required the harder work of crossing the internal territory first. He had to change the fabric of his own thought before he could change the external reality.

The article's practice recommendation is concrete and minimal: pause before agreeing or disagreeing; say 'Let me see if I understand you'; then reflect with 'It sounds like you are saying...' or 'It sounds like you are feeling...' followed by 'What did I get wrong?'
quotes: Most of us think we want to be understood. But what we really want is agreement.

Across 11 studies with 3,396 adults, speakers rated disagreeing listeners as worse listeners, even when those listeners showed real signs of listening. What this study tells us is that 'You're not listening' can often mean, 'You're not agreeing.'
When Sadat said he would go to Jerusalem, it sounded impossible. Then he went. An Egyptian Air Force jet touched down in Israel for the first time in history.
Sadat did not go to Jerusalem because he suddenly agreed with Israel. He went because he refused to let disagreement make understanding impossible.

He later wrote, 'He who cannot change the very fabric of his thought will never be able to change reality.' Before he could cross into enemy territory, he had to cross the harder territory within himself.
This is what understanding requires: the willingness to stay in the space between agree and disagree long enough to see what we could not see before.
